title: Plastic Antweight (1 lb All-Plastic) Combat Robots
scope_note: Complete reference for the 1 lb / 454 g all-plastic antweight combat robot class: exact ruleset wording and org-to-org variation on allowed/banned materials and metal exemptions, why the class exists, the dominant weapon/drive archetypes and why the plastic-only rule reshapes the meta, concrete build specs with per-part weight budgets, 3D printing material/settings/design-pattern practice, and where the community shares open-source designs.

entities.name: Plastic Antweight
entities.summary: A 1 lb (454 g) combat robot weight class in which structure, armor and weapons must be built from unmodified 3D-printable plastics (PLA/PLA+/PETG/ABS/ASA/PET), with metal permitted only for fasteners, motors, bearings, shafts, electronics and adhesives that do not themselves act as armor or weapon impactors.
entities.typical_arena: Same antweight arena as the standard 1lb class: a small (roughly 4x4 to 8x8 ft) Lexan/polycarbonate-walled box, run as its own bracket rather than mixed with metal antweights
entities.notes: Originated with Western Allied Robotics (WAR) in 2015 as an intentionally weaker-material 1lb class so that new builders could compete without CNC machining or metal fabrication. SPARC later formalized 'Plastic Classes' (section 4.4 of the SPARC Robot Construction Specifications) as a template most North American regional events now copy verbatim or with minor local amendments. It is functionally the same 454 g weight limit as a normal antweight; the only difference is the construction-material restriction. Some clubs also run a lighter plastic fairyweight/150g class, especially in the UK, which is a distinct weight bracket, not the same as the 1lb US plastic ant.

entities.name: SPARC Plastic Class (Robot Construction Specifications v1.6, §16.3)
entities.summary: The template ruleset most North American plastic-ant events build from. Defines the class's spirit, the exact allowed plastics list (verified verbatim against the current v1.6 PDF, 21 September 2025), the COTS-parts exemption with explicit permitted/not-permitted examples, and a notably strict post-processing ban.
entities.organization: SPARC (Standardized Procedures for the Advancement of Robotic Combat)
entities.version: v1.6, 21 September 2025, section 16.3 'Plastic Class' (this section was numbered §4.4 in older v1.4-era copies still quoted around the community; content is materially unchanged)
key_rules: 16.3 spirit (verbatim): 'The spirit of this class is to create an accessible and affordable class that encourages experimentation and rapid iteration by utilizing 3D printing.'
16.3.1.1 (verbatim): 'Frames, weapons and other custom parts may only be made from PLA, PLA+, PET, PETG, ABS, or ASA and must be FDM/FFF 3D printed.'
16.3.1.2 (verbatim): 'Materials that are functionally identical to PLA+ but have a different name for marketing purposes will be considered PLA+ when determining legality. (ex. PLA Pro, Super PLA)'

16.3.1.3/16.3.1.4 (verbatim): 'No other types of plastics or materials are allowed (ie. metal, carbon fiber, UHMW, etc). Composite and blended materials that use legal materials as a base are not permitted. Examples include but are not limited to: Carbon Fiber PLA, Glass Filled ABS, and Flex PLA.'

16.3.2.1 (verbatim, COTS exemption): 'Commercial Off The Shelf parts can be made from any material. This includes components such as motors, electronics, axles, bushings, bearings, fasteners, and adhesives.'

16.3.2.1.1 (verbatim, the actual policing test): 'COTS parts may not be used outside of their typically accepted function.' Permitted example given: 'Using shafts and bearings to allow wheels or a weapon to spin freely, using screws to attach two parts together.' Not-permitted example given: 'Using COTS parts as counterbalances for weapons, as weapon impactors, or as armor.'

16.3.2.1.2/16.3.2.1.3 (verbatim): COTS parts may be modified 'so long as the function of the part is not significantly changed' (e.g. shortening motor shafts, adding flats for set screws), and 'COTS equivalent parts are allowed' — builder-sourced/manufactured gearmotors, custom electronics, prototype components, and non-commercially-available axles all count as COTS-equivalent.
16.3.2.1.4 (verbatim): 'Magnets to enhance traction or downforce are prohibited.'

16.3.3 (wheels/tires, verbatim highlights): tires/traction elements may be COTS rubber, custom cast rubber, rubber coatings, or foam; parts between motor/shaft and tire must be COTS, foam, or printed from allowed materials; non-allowed-material traction elements 'may not be designed such that they provide more armor or structure than a COTS equivalent part.'

16.3.4 (verbatim, post-processing — notably strict): 'Painting or otherwise marking robots is permitted if done solely for aesthetic purposes... Post-processing of materials using techniques that enhance durability is not permitted. Disallowed processes include but are not limited to annealing, acetone soaking, and boiling of parts.'
16.3.5 (verbatim): 'Robots may be disqualified at the Event Organizer's discretion if it is deemed to violate the spirit of the class.'

Standard SPARC weight-bonus table applies on top (§4.1): 1lb/454g base, 1.25x (1.25lb) shuffler bonus, 1.5x (1.5lb) non-traditional-locomotion bonus, 2x (2lb) walker bonus — plastic ants can claim these bonuses exactly like standard-material antweights.

General SPARC safety rules apply on top: 60-second full manual deactivation (§3.4.3), visible weapon locking pin required at power-on (§3.4.6), drive fail-safe typically required even at 1lb (§6.4.1), at-least-two-frequency radio requirement (§6.4.2).
banned: any plastic not on the PLA/PLA+/PET/PETG/ABS/ASA list unless the organizer grants an exception
composite/blended filaments built on a legal base plastic (carbon-fiber PLA, glass-filled ABS, flex PLA, etc.)
COTS parts used as weapon counterbalance, weapon impactor, or armor
post-processing meant to enhance durability: annealing, acetone soaking, boiling of parts
entities.notes: This is the single most copy-pasted plastic-ant ruleset in the US; SCAR, Robot Ruckus and many one-off regional events either quote it directly or diverge from it in a clearly marked 'deviations' section per SPARC's own template instructions (§2). Notably, SPARC's own §16.3.4 explicitly BANS annealing/acetone-smoothing/boiling as illegal 'durability-enhancing' post-processing — a direct, verified contradiction with SCAR's separate Plastic Ant FAQ, which explicitly ALLOWS annealing and acid smoothing. This is real, current org-to-org variation, not a hypothetical: a part legally annealed for a SCAR event would need to be reprinted un-annealed to be legal at a strict-SPARC event, and vice versa is a non-issue since SPARC's list is the stricter one.

entities.name: SCAR 2025 Ruleset — Plastic Ant Weight Class
aliases: SoCal Attack Robots plastic ant rules
entities.summary: SoCal Attack Robots' 2025 ruleset section covering Plastic Ant, closely following SPARC's template but adding explicit weight bonuses for shufflers and non-wheeled locomotion and an explicit magnet/UHMW ban.
key_rules: Base weight 1lb / 454g; 1.25lb / 567g shuffler bonus; 1.5lb / 681g non-wheeled-motion bonus.
Structure, armor and weapons restricted to PET, PETG, ABS, ASA, PLA, or PLA+ (organizers may permit more at their discretion).
Motors, electronics, axles, fasteners and adhesives exempt from the plastic-only rule as long as they don't enhance structural integrity, armor, or weapon performance.
Metal, carbon fiber and UHMW explicitly prohibited as structural/armor/weapon material.
Magnets designed to boost traction or downforce are forbidden; foam is allowed for wheels and electronics padding.
Disqualification at event-organizer discretion for violating 'the spirit of the class'.

entities.name: SCAR Plastic Ant FAQ
entities.summary: A supplementary FAQ document SCAR publishes alongside its main ruleset that names specific approved filament brands and explicitly bans several materials (TPU, nylon, composites, epoxy coatings) that are ambiguous under the base ruleset's plain-language material list.
key_rules: Chassis/weapon material must be PLA, ABS, or PETG printable under 260°C; named approved brands include FusionFilaments HTPLA+, Duramic PLA+, Overture Super PLA+, and Hatchbox ABS.

COTS wheel parts (e.g. FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, Pololu) are allowed, along with COTS rubber, cast urethane, foam, or rubber coatings and traction additives (silicone/latex) for tires, unless they create entanglement risk.
Metal bearings, axles, shafts, fasteners, COTS motor-mount adapters, and metal servo horns/gears are exempted as long as the weapon is non-functional without its plastic parts.
Post-processing: annealing or smoothing with heat or acid is allowed, thin decorative paint is allowed; material additives are not.
Inspection is primarily visual; datasheets are not required by default, but suspicious builds can be investigated further.
banned: TPU, including custom TPU wheel hubs
'flex' or blended filaments marketed for enhanced properties
epoxy coatings, Bondo, or similar fillers
entities.notes:
IMPORTANT ORG-VARIANCE FINDING #1: SCAR is one of the stricter interpreters of the plastic-only rule on MATERIALS — it explicitly bans TPU and nylon by name, materials that are commonly praised in general antweight/beetleweight circles as tough flexible armor. Builders moving a design between events must check the local FAQ, not just the base material list, since 'PETG/PLA/ABS' alone does not settle whether TPU trim or nylon gears are legal.

IMPORTANT ORG-VARIANCE FINDING #2 (verified against both primary sources directly): SCAR's FAQ explicitly ALLOWS 'annealing or smoothing with heat or acid,' while SPARC's current v1.6 Robot Construction Specifications (§16.3.4) explicitly BANS annealing, acetone soaking, and boiling as illegal 'durability-enhancing' post-processing. This is a direct, confirmed contradiction between two real, currently-published plastic-ant rulesets on the exact same question — a concrete case where a part legal at one event is illegal at another with no visual difference at inspection time, entirely dependent on which ruleset the event runs.

entities.name: Western Allied Robotics (WAR) Plastic Antweight — Original 2015 Rules
entities.summary: The founding ruleset of the plastic antweight class, introduced by Western Allied Robotics in 2015, restricting the chassis and weapon to PET/PETG/ABS/PLA/PLA+ while exempting motors, electronics, axles, fasteners and adhesives.
entities.version: 2015 origin ruleset (language subsequently absorbed into SPARC §4.4)
key_rules: 1lb weight limit, same as standard antweight.
Chassis and weapon restricted to PET, PETG, ABS, PLA, PLA+.
Motors, electronics, axles, fasteners, adhesives exempt from the material restriction provided they don't add structural strength, armor, or weapon performance.
Robot competes in a separate plastic-only bracket, never mixed with standard-material antweights.
banned: metal or any non-listed plastic used as chassis/armor/weapon material
entities.notes: This WAR wording is essentially word-for-word what became SPARC section 4.4, making WAR the direct ancestor of nearly every plastic-ant ruleset now in use.

entities.name: Robot Ruckus Plastic Ant Construction Rules
entities.summary: Robot Ruckus's plastic ant rules, requiring 3D-printed PLA/PLA+/ABS/PETG construction and following the standard metal-fastener exemption, with an explicit requirement that surface screws be countersunk or shrouded so they cannot act as armor or weapon impactors.
key_rules: Plastic Ant robots must be 3D printed in PLA, PLA+, ABS or PETG.
Non-plastic parts (motors, electronics, axles, fasteners, adhesives) may be any material but cannot enhance structural integrity, armor, or weapon performance.
Metal fasteners are allowed, but where they appear on the outer surface they should be countersunk or shrouded so they cannot act as an impact point or armor plate.
banned: metal, carbon fiber or other non-approved material used structurally, as armor, or as a weapon surface
exposed/proud metal fastener heads used as de facto armor studs

entities.name: Plastic Ant Vertical Spinner
entities.summary: The single most common competitive plastic-ant archetype: a spinning disc or drum on a vertical (side-to-side relative to the arena floor, striking-face-forward) axis, printed from PETG or ABS, driven by a small brushless outrunner. Dominant because a thick printed disc keeps its weapon mass close to the axis and hits with blunt, ring-shaped force rather than requiring a hardened cutting edge.
entities.typical_weapon_motor: Small brushless outrunner, roughly 1811-2205 size, 1900-2800kv, run on 2S
entities.typical_drive: Two micro brushed gearmotors (N20 or 130-size) direct-driving small printed/TPU-tired wheels
pros: Printed disc/hub is simple to design and cheap to replace after a broken tooth or crack
Blunt ring impact matches what plastic can survive better than a thin blade
Good self-righting behavior if the disc doubles as a bumper
cons: Printed weapon can crack or delaminate at the bore/keyway under repeated hits
Needs a well-designed containment/guard since a plastic disc can shatter more unpredictably than metal
Kinetic energy per gram is inherently lower than a metal disc of the same size
entities.notes: Because printed plastic is roughly 3-6x less dense and far weaker in tension than hardened steel, plastic-ant vertical spinners spend a disproportionate share of the 454g budget on the disc/hub and its surrounding shroud rather than on drive power.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Drum Spinner (Undercutter)
entities.summary: A full-width horizontal drum, usually printed in PETG for impact ductility, spun on an axis parallel to the ground and low to the floor to drive under opponents. The drum's wall thickness itself does the damage (blunt/ram) rather than teeth, and the wide printed cylinder is naturally stronger against delamination than a thin bar.
entities.typical_weapon_motor: Brushless outrunner 1811-2204 size, 2600-3000kv on 2S, occasionally geared down slightly for torque
entities.typical_drive: Two micro gearmotors, often mounted to keep the drum as low to the ground as possible
pros: A full cylindrical drum wall resists cracking better than a thin bar because load is spread around the ring
Low profile makes it hard for wedges to get underneath
Printed teeth/paddles on the drum are cheap to reprint after being chipped
cons: Full-width weapon leaves the whole front exposed; a chip anywhere can unbalance the drum
Needs precise balancing since a small amount of unbalanced printed mass vibrates badly at high RPM
entities.notes: Popular open-source design (e.g. the community 'drum spinner combat robot' shared on Printables) demonstrates the class's move away from bar spinners toward drums for exactly this durability reason.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Horizontal (Bar) Spinner
entities.summary: A single spinning bar or blade on a vertical axis (spinning in the horizontal plane, striking outward in a circle), the dominant weapon type in metal antweight but a comparatively weak and fragile choice in plastic because the weapon tip itself must be printed plastic rather than hardened steel.
entities.typical_weapon_motor: Brushless outrunner 1400-2000kv on 2S-3S (lower kv than vertical spinners to keep tip speed in a survivable range for the printed blade)
pros: Can hit from any side without needing to line up a face, useful defensively
Simple single-part weapon geometry is easy to print and swap
cons: A thin printed bar tip is the weakest possible cross-section in the weakest material allowed in the class — it is the archetype most likely to shatter on its own first hit
Raises the robot's center of gravity and exposes a large flat profile for wedges/lifters to exploit
Kinetic energy transfer to the opponent is poor compared to metal because the bar has to be kept thick (hence slower or lighter) to survive its own swing
entities.notes: This is the archetype most changed by the plastic-only rule. In metal antweight, bar spinners with hardened steel or titanium tips are a top-tier weapon; in plastic, the same geometry with a printed tip is fragile and prone to catastrophic self-destruction, which is a large part of why drums and vertical spinners with thick printed hubs dominate the plastic meta instead.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Beater Bar / Egg-beater
entities.summary: A low, wide horizontal weapon bar mounted close to the floor at the front of the robot that beats upward into an opponent's underside, similar in geometry to a drum spinner but usually a simpler bar rather than a full cylinder, printed thick to survive repeated low-clearance strikes.
entities.typical_drive: Two micro gearmotors, low ground clearance chassis
pros: Cheaper/simpler to print than a full drum
Low profile discourages opposing wedges
cons: Narrower than a drum so it can miss off-center hits
Bar ends are a stress concentration point that tends to crack first

entities.name: Plastic Ant Wedge / Control Bot
entities.summary: A weaponless or lightly-weaponed robot built around a low front wedge and strong drivetrain, designed to win on driving skill, ring-out and judges' decision rather than weapon damage — often the recommended first build and a strong beginner-friendly counter to fragile plastic spinners.
entities.typical_weapon_motor: none, or a small servo-driven active wedge/lifter
entities.typical_drive: Two drive motors sized for torque over top speed, direct-drive to grippy TPU-tired wheels
pros: Nothing to break: no weapon motor, ESC, or fragile printed weapon to crack
Thick printed wedge is one of the best uses of plastic's weight-cheap bulk
Excellent way to learn driving and electronics before adding a weapon
Directly counters the fragile plastic-only spinner archetypes by denying them a clean hit
cons: Cannot win by knockout/damage, relies on ring-outs, pins and judges' decisions
Loses to a well-driven spinner that gets underneath or around the wedge
entities.notes: Almost every 'first plastic ant' guide recommends starting here because the failure mode (a cracked wedge) is a five-minute reprint, unlike a broken weapon motor mount.

entities.name: Plastic Ant Lifter
entities.summary: A wedge-fronted robot with a servo- or small-motor-actuated arm that scoops and lifts an opponent to expose their underside or throw them, using printed linkages instead of the pneumatics common in bigger lifters.
entities.typical_weapon_motor: Micro servo or small geared DC motor with a printed cam/linkage, occasionally a rubber-band-assisted snap lift
entities.typical_drive: Two drive motors on printed wheels
pros: Can win by control and occasional big flips without needing a fast-spinning weapon
Lift arm doubles as self-righting mechanism
cons: Printed linkage pins/hinges wear and can strip under repeated combat loads
Slower to act than a spinner, needs good positioning

entities.name: N20 Micro Gearmotor (6-12V)
entities.summary: A tiny brushed DC gearmotor in a roughly 12x10x10mm metal gearbox, the most common drive motor in plastic antweights due to its low cost, light weight, and wide range of stock gear ratios.
entities.vendor: various (generic/AliExpress/Amazon; also sold by hobby motor shops)
pros: Very cheap and widely available
Metal gearbox is more durable than plastic-gear toy motors
Many stock gear ratios (from ~30 RPM crawlers to 1000+ RPM speedsters)
cons: Low torque compared to bigger motors, limits ramming power
Output shaft can shear under sudden weapon-strike shock loads if used for anything but drive
entities.notes:
Realistic weight range 9-12g depending on gear ratio; price typically $3-5 each bought in bulk.

Generic N20 form factors vary substantially by winding, ratio, shaft, gearbox internals, and supplier. Use a specific motor record for numeric design work.

entities.name: 130-Size Brushed Drive Motor
entities.summary: A classic small brushed can motor (the same family used in cheap toy cars) sometimes paired with a 3D-printed or small stock gearbox for antweight drive; cheaper and more available than purpose-built combat drive motors.
pros: Extremely cheap
High no-load RPM gives room for a wide range of gear ratios
cons: Needs a separate gearbox (adds weight/complexity) since raw RPM is too high for direct drive
Lower quality bearings than purpose-made combat motors
entities.notes: 130-size is a motor envelope/class, not one winding or performance specification.

entities.name: Micro Brushless Outrunner, ~2600KV (1811-size class)
entities.summary: A small brushless outrunner motor in the size class commonly used for antweight vertical spinner and drum weapons, run on 2S LiPo for a good balance of RPM and torque within a plastic ant's weight and tip-speed goals.
entities.vendor: various (e.g. hobby drone-motor brands repurposed for combat)
pros: Good RPM-to-weight ratio for spinning a light printed disc/drum
Widely available from hobby drone/FPV suppliers
cons: Needs a compatible brushless ESC and careful gearing/direct-drive sizing to avoid over-revving a plastic weapon past its burst speed
entities.notes:
2800kv is commonly cited as a 'vertical spinner' sweet spot kv in community guides; 1400kv is more typical for slower horizontal spinners.

This is a nominal-KV reference class, not a specific SKU; mass, current, voltage rating, shaft and mounting vary by motor.

entities.name: Micro Brushless Outrunner, ~1400KV
entities.summary: A lower-kv small outrunner used for horizontal/bar spinners and drums where more torque and a lower tip speed (kinder to a printed weapon) is preferred over raw RPM.
pros: Lower RPM is easier on a printed weapon's burst strength
More torque for heavier drums
cons: Lower tip speed means less kinetic energy transfer per hit
entities.notes: This is a nominal-KV reference class, not a specific SKU; mass, current, voltage rating, shaft and mounting vary by motor.

entities.name: Micro Brushless Weapon ESC (~6A)
entities.summary: A tiny brushless ESC (often an AM32 or BLHeli-based FPV-drone-derived board) used to run the weapon motor in a plastic ant, valued for its very low weight relative to the alternative of a brushed weapon motor and controller.
pros: Extremely light
Programmable spin-up behavior (some support instant full throttle at arm for combat)
cons: Small package can be sensitive to heat if run continuously at max current
Needs correct motor-timing configuration for reliable spin-up under weapon load
entities.notes: Representative micro-ESC class only; firmware, voltage range, real thermal current capability and mass depend on the exact board.

entities.name: Micro Combo RX + Dual Brushed ESC Board
entities.summary: An all-in-one micro PCB combining a radio receiver with two small brushed motor drivers, the standard drive-electronics solution in antweights because it saves the weight and wiring of separate RX and ESC boards.
pros: One part instead of three (receiver + two ESCs), saving weight and wiring
Common failsafe-on-signal-loss behavior built in, satisfying rules requiring drive failsafe
cons: If it fails, the whole robot loses both drive and radio at once
Current rating (often 2-4A per channel) can limit motor choice
entities.notes: Generic combo-board concept. Use a specific Malenki, Catalyst, or other exact board record for ratings.

entities.name: 2S 300mAh LiPo Battery
entities.summary: A small 2-cell lithium polymer pack, the most common power source for plastic ant vertical spinner and drum builds, giving 7.4V nominal for both a brushless weapon motor and brushed drive motors.
pros: Good energy density for the weight
Widely available in the FPV-drone hobby supply chain
cons: Requires a LiPo-safe charger and storage practice
Capacity/runtime trade-off against the 454g total weight budget
entities.notes: Capacity/cell count define this reference class; mass, C-rating, connector and price vary by pack.

entities.name: 1S 300-500mAh LiPo Battery
entities.summary: A single-cell LiPo pack used in budget or control-focused plastic ants running low-voltage brushed drive motors without a brushless weapon.
pros: Lightest common battery option, frees weight budget for armor
Cheapest LiPo option
cons: Only suitable for low-voltage drive motors and small brushed weapon setups, not brushless spinners
entities.notes: Reference class only; exact mass, discharge rating and connector depend on the pack.

entities.name: Printed Hub + TPU Tire Wheel
entities.summary: A 3D-printed rigid hub (PLA+/PETG) with a separately printed TPU tire pressed or glued on, the standard plastic-ant wheel: fully print-and-replace, and legal everywhere since both hub and tire are on the approved plastic list (subject to local TPU rulings).
pros: Essentially free once you own a printer and TPU spool
Easy to redesign tread pattern for grip
Print-and-replace after wear or damage
cons: TPU is explicitly banned by some events (e.g. SCAR); always check local rules before relying on it
Lower grip than purpose-made silicone/foam tires unless tread is well designed
entities.notes: Representative component class; use an exact part/drawing before relying on dimensions, weight, rating or price.

entities.name: COTS Foam/Silicone Antweight Wheel
entities.summary: An off-the-shelf foam or silicone-tired wheel (e.g. FingerTech, Repeat Robotics, Pololu) explicitly allowed as a non-plastic-restricted exemption for wheels/tires under most plastic-ant rulesets, offering better and more consistent grip than a printed tire.
pros: Consistent, well-tested grip
No printing/gluing labor
Explicitly named as legal by SCAR's FAQ regardless of the plastic-only rule
cons: Costs more than a printed wheel
Less customizable diameter/tread than a printed part
entities.notes: Representative component class; use an exact part/drawing before relying on dimensions, weight, rating or price.

entities.name: Small Flanged Ball Bearing (3-4mm bore)
entities.summary: A tiny flanged metal bearing used to support a plastic ant's weapon shaft, explicitly allowed as a metal exemption in every plastic-ant ruleset since bearings are functional hardware, not armor or weapon surface.
pros: Cheap and standardized sizes
Explicitly rules-legal as a metal component in every plastic-ant ruleset reviewed
cons: Needs a properly toleranced printed bore to press-fit without cracking the surrounding plastic
entities.notes: Representative component class; use an exact part/drawing before relying on dimensions, weight, rating or price.

entities.name: Small-Diameter Steel Weapon Shaft
entities.summary: A short length of steel drill rod or precision shaft used to carry a plastic weapon disc/drum, exempt from the plastic-only rule as an 'axle' under SPARC-derived language as long as it does not itself act as an armor surface or weapon edge.
pros: Much stiffer and more wear-resistant than a printed shaft would be
Explicitly allowed as an axle exemption in every ruleset reviewed
cons: Must be fully shrouded by the printed weapon body so it can't be argued to be acting as a metal weapon tip
entities.notes: Representative component class; use an exact part/drawing before relying on dimensions, weight, rating or price.

entities.name: M2/M3 Screws + Heat-Set Threaded Inserts
entities.summary: Small metal machine screws combined with brass heat-set threaded inserts melted into printed holes, the standard plastic-ant fastening method, explicitly allowed everywhere as long as screw heads on outer surfaces are countersunk or shrouded rather than left proud as de facto armor studs.
pros: Reusable threads in soft plastic (printed threads alone strip quickly)
Universally rules-legal metal exemption
cons: Requires a soldering iron or heat-set tool to install inserts
Proud/exposed screw heads on the outer shell can draw a rules objection if not countersunk (per Robot Ruckus wording)
entities.notes: Representative component class; use an exact part/drawing before relying on dimensions, weight, rating or price.

entities.name: Micro Slide/Toggle Power Switch
entities.summary: A small mechanical switch used as the required manual main power disconnect, mounted in a printed slot so it can be actuated without contacting moving parts, satisfying the SPARC-derived 15-second manual-disconnect rule.
pros: Cheap, simple, satisfies safety inspection requirements
cons: Must be positioned so it can be reached without risk from a still-armed weapon
entities.notes: Representative component class; use an exact part/drawing before relying on dimensions, weight, rating or price.

entities.name: PLA+ (Modified PLA)
entities.summary: A modified PLA filament formulation marketed for improved impact resistance over standard PLA while keeping PLA's easy printability, one of the five materials SPARC and SCAR explicitly name as legal for plastic-ant chassis and weapons.
entities.machinability: Excellent for FDM printing; low warp, prints cool (190-215C typical), poor for post-print machining
pros: Easiest of the legal plastics to print reliably
Rarely warps, good for small precise parts
Explicitly legal in every plastic-ant ruleset reviewed
cons: Still more brittle than PETG/ABS under sharp impact despite the '+' marketing
Lower heat resistance than PETG/ABS

entities.name: PETG
entities.summary: A tougher, more impact-ductile filament than PLA, widely considered the best default choice for plastic-ant weapon discs/drums and load-bearing chassis members because it bends and absorbs energy rather than shattering.
entities.machinability: Prints slightly hotter than PLA (230-250C), can string more, but layer adhesion is strong
pros: Best combination of legal-everywhere status and real-world impact toughness
More heat resistant than PLA (useful near weapon-motor heat)
Ductile failure mode (bends/cracks slowly) instead of shattering
cons: More prone to stringing/oozing than PLA, needs tuned retraction settings
Slightly heavier per volume than PLA/ABS

entities.name: ABS
entities.summary: A strong, impact-resistant, comparatively low-density filament, one of the five universally-legal plastic-ant materials; harder to print reliably (needs an enclosure to prevent warping) but rewards the effort with a lighter, tougher part than PLA.
use_cases: chassis shells where weight savings matter
entities.machinability: Needs an enclosed/heated-chamber printer to avoid warping; can be acetone-vapor-smoothed for extra surface strength
pros: Lowest density of the commonly-used legal plastics, saving weight for the same part size
Very impact resistant when printed well
Acetone-smoothable, which can weld layer lines together for extra strength
cons: Warps badly without an enclosure and a heated bed
Fumes require ventilation
Less beginner-friendly than PLA/PETG

entities.name: TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane)
entities.summary: A rubber-like flexible printable filament popular in the wider combat-robot community for flexible armor panels and wheel tires because it bends and springs back instead of cracking — but it is NOT on the standard SPARC/SCAR approved-material list and is explicitly banned by name in SCAR's FAQ, making it a key org-to-org variance point in the plastic-ant class.
entities.machinability: Prints slowly, needs direct-drive extruder, high flexibility makes it hard to feed through bowden setups
pros: Excellent energy absorption; deflects and springs back rather than cracking
Great for wheel tires and shock-mounts when the local ruleset allows it
cons: NOT on the base SPARC 4.4.1 list (PET/PETG/ABS/PLA/PLA+ only) unless an organizer grants an explicit exception
Explicitly named as banned by SCAR's Plastic Ant FAQ, including for wheel hubs
entities.notes: Builders should never assume TPU is legal in a plastic-ant event just because it's a 3D-printed plastic — check the specific event's material list or FAQ before designing it in.

entities.name: Nylon (Printed)
entities.summary: A tough, wear-resistant, semi-flexible printable nylon filament that, like TPU, sits outside the base SPARC 4.4.1 approved list and is explicitly banned by name in SCAR's plastic ant FAQ, despite being a popular choice for gears and living-hinge parts in general 3D-printing use.
use_cases: gears and wear parts (in general 3D printing, not this class)
entities.machinability: Hygroscopic (absorbs moisture, needs dry storage/drying before printing), prints hot
pros: Very tough and abrasion-resistant in general use
cons: Explicitly banned by SCAR's plastic ant FAQ
Not on the SPARC baseline approved list either
Moisture-sensitive, harder to print reliably than PLA/PETG/ABS

entities.name: Force Knight — Open-Source 1lb Plastic Antweight
entities.summary: A free, open-source 1lb plastic antweight design by community builder Michael K, published as downloadable STL files on Printables and described as intended for SCAR-legal component kits — a good example of the fully-open designs the plastic ant scene shares.

entities.name: CRNZ Antweight Combat Robot Kit
entities.summary: An open-source printable antweight chassis kit published by CombatRoboticsNZ on Thingiverse, designed to be extensible and modular so builders can swap weapon and drive modules without redesigning the whole robot.

entities.name: Legally Distinct — Open-Source 150g UK Drum Spinner Design
entities.summary: A free printable 150g UK-class antweight drum-spinner design by community builder Blessy (published on Thingiverse and documented on Hackaday.io), explicitly built as an homage/iteration on the established UK drum spinner 'Siren' — a clear, verified illustration of how the plastic scene iterates openly on successful designs.

Concrete build details (verified via the Hackaday.io project page): drive uses 2x N20 gearmotors (~600rpm class), the drum weapon motor mount is sized for a BE1806 2300kv brushless motor with a 3mm bearing on the opposite side of the drum, and the design runs a 'malenki nano' micro ESC (a BBB Dual ESC was noted as a possible but tighter-fitting swap). The design iterated through weight: V2.1 was reported ~4g over the 150g limit, and V3.1 was revised to cut weight and reportedly finished at ~139g — a real example of the iterate-and-reprint weight-budget process that defines the plastic-ant/printable-ant design culture at any scale.

entities.name: Siren (UK 150g Antweight / US Fairyweight)
entities.summary: A 150g UK-Antweight/US-Fairyweight drum-spinner combat robot by designer drcameron, published as free STL files on Thingiverse and Cults3D, well-known enough in the printable-antweight scene to have directly inspired the open-source 'Legally Distinct' drum spinner.
achievements: Directly credited as the design inspiration for the widely-built Thingiverse/Hackaday.io 'Legally Distinct' plastic drum spinner
